chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Isa ibn al-Qasim, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who became junub in the month of Ramadan at the beginning of the night, so he delayed the bath until dawn rose. He said: 'He completes his fast and there is no qada (make-up) upon him.'
And from him, from al-Nufayli, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Sulayman ibn Abi Zaynab, who said:

I wrote to Abu al-Hasan Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon them both), asking him about a man who became junub in the month of Ramadan from the beginning of the night, so he delayed the bath until dawn rose. He (peace be upon him) wrote to me in his own handwriting: 'I know it, just like one who is coincidentally delayed, he bathes from his junub state and completes his fast and there is nothing upon him.'

key_terms.أَجْنَبَ: Became ritually impure (junub) due to major impurity
key_terms.مُصَادِفٍ: Coincidentally delayed / one who is delayed by circumstance

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on fasting if one becomes junub and delays ghusl until dawn in Ramadan?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the juristic consensus among the Imams that delaying *ghusl* until dawn does not invalidate the Ramadan fast, distinguishing this state from intentional eating or drinking. It underscores the Shia principle that ritual purity is a condition for prayer validity rather than fast validity, provided the impurity is not due to deliberate consumption of food or drink. This ruling alleviates the burden on worshippers who may be delayed in performing their ritual bath, emphasizing ease in religious obligations.
